## Intro:

Logicals, i.e., *Logical vectors*, are powerfuls ways to transform, filter or subset our data. Here we derive the basics using tricks from the `tidyverse`, as per `R for data science`, and showcase the equivalents using `polars` in python.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
dat <- starwars
# readr::write_csv(dat, "Data/R4DS/starwars.csv")

```

```{python}
import polars as pl
import pandas as pd
import polars.selectors as cs

dat_pl = pl.read_csv("Data/R4DS/starwars.csv")
```

### Comparison:

- Some simple things from the ground up: how does `dplyr::filter()` and `polars.filter()` work under the hood?

- Imagine we want to filter out specific rows in the `starwars` data set, e.g., characters with blue eyes:

```{r}
dat |> 
    filter(eye_color == "blue") |> 
    select(name, eye_color)
```

```{python}
(
    dat_pl
    .filter(pl.col("eye_color") == "blue")
    .select(pl.col("name"), pl.col("eye_color"))
)
```

- Alright, easy! But what is actually happening here? Under the hood, both R and python use a logical vector, and it filters (selects) everywehere this is `TRUE` (in R) and `True` (in python):

```{r}
dat |> 
    mutate(blue_eye_color = eye_color == "blue") |> 
    select(name, eye_color, blue_eye_color) |> 
    filter(blue_eye_color) |> 
    select(!blue_eye_color)
```

```{python}
(
    dat_pl
    .with_columns(blue_eye_color = pl.col("eye_color") == "blue")
    .select("name", "eye_color", "blue_eye_color")
    .filter(pl.col("blue_eye_color"))
    .drop("blue_eye_color")
)
```

### `base::is.na()`

- One important thing to note is that in R and python, `NA` or `Na` or `Null` are missing values. Usally a filtering function drops missing values:

```{r}
dat |> select(mass)

# Show NA's
dat |> filter(mass == NA)
dat |> filter(is.na(mass))

```

- Note that we cant use `== NA`. `NA` is a missing value, it cant be equal to anything because we don't know the value: As per R4DS:
```{r}
age_person_1 <- NA
age_person_2 <- NA

age_person_1 == age_person_2
``` 

- This becomes `NA` because we don't know the values!

### `polars.is_null()`

- In `polars` we use `is_null()`

```{python}
(
    dat_pl
    .filter(pl.col("mass").is_null())
)
```

- What?! Why 0 rows?! Looking at the data we obviously have `NA` in our data!

```{python}
(
    dat_pl
    .filter(pl.col("mass") == "NA")
)
```

- Okey, so this actually stems from HOW we read in the `.csv` file in the first place! Check this

```{python}
dat_pl = pl.read_csv("Data/R4DS/starwars.csv", null_values = "NA")

(
    dat_pl
    .filter(pl.col("mass").is_null())
)
```

- Another difference between R and Pythons behaviour is that in R, `NA's` usually go to the bottom of a data frame when we sort it:

```{r}
dat |> 
    filter(eye_color == "blue") |> 
    arrange(desc(mass))

# We can override this using is.na
dat |> 
    filter(eye_color == "blue") |> 
    arrange(desc(is.na(mass)), desc(mass))
```

- In python `null` is a the top straight away:

```{python}
(
    dat_pl
    .filter(pl.col("eye_color") == "blue")
    .sort(pl.col("mass"), descending = True)
)

# Overrid to match R's default:
(
    dat_pl
    .filter(pl.col("eye_color") == "blue")
    .sort(pl.col("mass").is_null(), pl.col("mass"), descending = [False, True])
)
```

- Also, the `%in%` operator in R and the `.is_in()` operator in polars are special:

```{r}
dat |> filter(homeworld %in% c("Tatooine", "Alderaan"))
```

```{python}
(
    dat_pl
    .filter(pl.col("homeworld").is_in(["Tatooine", "Alderaan"]))
)
```

- What the `%in%` and `.is_in()` operators does is that it basically checks `col == condition_1 | col == condition_2`.

### Logical summaries: `base::any()` & `base::all()`

- In R, `base::any()` and `base::all()` returns `TRUE` or `FALSE` given the condition supplied

```{r}
dat |> 
    summarise(
        any_blue_eyes = any(eye_color == "blue"),
        all_blue_eyes = all(eye_color == "blue"),
        .by = homeworld
    )
```

- In Python:

```{python}
(
    dat_pl.group_by("homeworld", maintain_order = True).agg(
        any_blue_eyes = (pl.col("eye_color") == "blue").any(ignore_nulls = False),
        all_blue_eyes = (pl.col("eye_color") == "blue").all(ignore_nulls = False)
    )
)
```

### Numerical summaries of logicals:

- As per R4DS, using logicals on numeric vectors implies that `TRUE` becomes `1` and `FALSE` becomes `0`. We can use this to get counts and proportions of `TRUES`:

```{r}
dat |> 
    mutate(
        height_m = height / 100,
        bmi = (mass / height_m^2),
        class = bmi >= 30
    ) |> 
    select(name, height, height_m, mass, bmi, class) |> 
    summarise(
        prop = mean(class, na.rm = TRUE),
        count = sum(class, na.rm = TRUE)
    )

dat |> 
    mutate(
        height_m = height / 100,
        bmi = (mass / height_m^2)
    ) |> 
    summarise(
        prop = mean(bmi >= 30, na.rm = TRUE),
        count = sum(bmi >= 30, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
```

- Using python:

```{python}
(
    dat_pl
    .with_columns(height_m = pl.col("height") / 100)
    .with_columns(bmi = (pl.col("mass") / pl.col("height_m")**2))
    .with_columns(pl.col("bmi").ge(30).alias("class"))
    .select("name", "height", "height_m", "mass", "bmi", "class")
    # Note that we can't use .agg on a polars df, we need to use select:
    .select(
        pl.col("class").mean().alias("mean"),
        pl.col("class").sum().alias("count")
    )
)

(
    dat_pl
    .with_columns(height_m = pl.col("height") / 100)
    .with_columns((pl.col("mass") / pl.col("height_m") ** 2).alias("bmi"))
    .select(
        prop = (pl.col("bmi").ge(30)).mean(),
        count = pl.col("bmi").ge(30).sum()
    )
)
```

- Let's mix it up and group by `gender`:

```{r}
# First way:
dat |> 
    mutate(
        height_m = height / 100,
        bmi = mass / height_m^2
    ) |>
    summarise(
        prop = mean(bmi >= 30, na.rm = TRUE),
        count = sum(bmi >= 30, na.rm = TRUE),
        .by = gender
    )

# Second way:
dat |> 
    mutate(
        height_m = height / 100,
        bmi = mass / height_m^2
    ) |> 
    group_by(gender) |> 
    summarise(
        prop = mean(bmi >= 30, na.rm = TRUE),
        count = sum(bmi >= 30, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
    )
```

- And in python:

```{python}
(
    dat_pl
    .with_columns(height_m = pl.col("height") / 100)
    .with_columns((pl.col("mass") / pl.col("height_m") ** 2).alias("bmi"))
    .group_by("gender")
    .agg(
        (pl.col("bmi").ge(30)).mean().alias("prop"),
        (pl.col("bmi").ge(30)).sum().alias("count")
    )
)

```

- Note one difference: in `polars` we don't need to ungroup the data like we do when we use `dplyr`. Or rather, in `dplyr` we don't NEED to ungroup the data - however it is good practice do to so! Using `summarise` we can use the `.by = ` arguement, which works like `.group_by()` in polars, i.e., once the summary is done, groups are dropped. If we use `group_by()` before a `summarise()` function, we should also include a `.groups = "drop"` argument or pipe in a `ungroup()` function after the summary: `summarise(...) |> ungroup()`

### Logical subsetting:

- As per R4DS we can also use logicals to filter, or subset, the data before summarising (aggregating) data. In R we use the `subset` operator, `[`, which is quite reminicent of how `pandas` subsets data.

```{r}
# First way: use group_by to keep up between languages
dat |> 
    filter(eye_color == "blue") |> 
    group_by(gender) |> 
    summarise(
        mean_weight = mean(mass, na.rm = TRUE),
        n = n(),
        .groups = "drop"
    )

# Second way: Note however that that it's one the mean that gets the subsetted data
dat |> 
    group_by(gender) |> 
    summarise(
        mean_weight = mean(mass[eye_color == "blue"], na.rm = TRUE),
        n = sum(eye_color == "blue", na.rm = TRUE), # Can't use n = n() here beacuse it can't be subsetted!
        n_tot = n(),
        .groups = "drop"
    )
```

- Using `polars`:

```{python}
# First way:
(
    dat_pl.filter(pl.col("eye_color") == "blue")
    .group_by("gender")
    .agg(
        mean_weight = pl.col("mass").mean(), 
        n = pl.len()
    )
)

(
    dat_pl
    .group_by("gender")
    .agg(
        mean_weight = pl.col("mass").filter(pl.col("eye_color") == "blue").mean(),
        n = (pl.col("eye_color") == "blue").sum(),
        n_tot = pl.len()
    )
)
```

### Logical transformation:

- Now probably the most important part: How to create logicals that we can use!

- In R, we typically use `if_else()` and `case_when()` for creating logicals. In python, we typically use `pl.when().then().otherwise()` chain method

```{r}
# 1. if_else()
sw |> 
    mutate(
        height_m = height / 100,
        bmi = mass / height_m^2,
        obesitas = if_else(bmi >= 30, "Yes", "No"),
        .keep = "used"
    )

# 2. nested if_else()
sw |> 
    mutate(
        height_m = height / 100,
        bmi = mass / height_m^2,
        obesitas = if_else(
            bmi >= 30 & bmi < 35, "Yes, class 1", if_else(
                bmi >= 35 & bmi < 40, "Yes, class 2", if_else(
                    bmi >= 40, "Yes, class 3", "No"
                )
            ) 
        ), , .keep = "used"
    ) |> print(n = Inf)
```

- This works fine. But it's far from perfect. First thing to note is that a nested `if_else()` should be used as a last resort! A better solution is to utilze `case_when()`:

```{r}
sw |> 
    mutate(
        height_m = height / 100,
        bmi = mass / height_m^2,
        obesitas = case_when(
            bmi >= 30 & bmi < 35 ~ "Yes, class 1",
            bmi >= 35 & bmi < 40 ~ "Yes, class 2",
            bmi >= 40 ~ "Yes, class 3",
            .default  = "No"
        ), .keep = "used"
    ) |> print(n = Inf)
```

- This is much easier to read, and much easier to write!

- Turning to `Polars`:

```{python}
(
    dat_pl
    .with_columns((pl.col("height") / 100).alias("height_m"))
    .with_columns((pl.col("mass") / pl.col("height_m")**2).alias("bmi"))
    .with_columns(
        obesitas = pl.when(pl.col("bmi") >= 30).then(pl.lit("Yes"))
        .otherwise(pl.lit("No")))
)

(
    dat_pl
    .with_columns(height_m = (pl.col("height") / 100))
    .with_columns(bmi = (pl.col("mass") / pl.col("height_m")**2))
    .with_columns(
        obesitas = pl.when((pl.col("bmi") >= 30) & (pl.col("bmi") < 35)).then(pl.lit("Yes, class 1"))
        .when((pl.col("bmi") >= 35) & (pl.col("bmi") < 40)).then(pl.lit("Yes, class 2"))
        .when(pl.col("bmi") >= 40).then(pl.lit("Yes, class 3"))
        .otherwise(pl.lit("No"))
    )
)
```
